planting.note: Plant seedlings or container-grown trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained loam in full sun to partial shade; this classic European mountain fir resents shallow, dry, or chalky soils.

directions: European silver fir is a tall, straight-trunked mountain conifer from central and southern Europe, with flat, glossy dark-green needles showing two bright white stomatal bands on their undersides. It was once the dominant Christmas tree of continental Europe before Nordmann fir largely displaced it, and it remains valued in large landscapes and arboreta for its stately form and smooth gray bark. Give it deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil and cool, humid conditions, since it performs poorly in compacted, waterlogged, or drought-prone sites. Older specimens develop a broad, flat-topped crown quite different from the narrow spire of young trees.
sources: The Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in cool, moist, well-drained acidic soil in full sun; Veitch fir is a high-elevation species that needs cool summers and struggles in hot, humid, or dry climates.

directions: Veitch fir is a Japanese mountain conifer named for the Veitch nursery dynasty that introduced it to Western gardens in the 1860s, prized for the vivid silvery-white undersides of its short, upturned needles that flash brightly when the branches sway. It forms a narrow, symmetrical spire and is a favorite specimen tree in cool-summer collections and conifer gardens where few other firs thrive. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil with reliable moisture, and avoid hot, humid lowland sites, since this fir is adapted to cold, snowy subalpine slopes on Honshu. Purple young cones held upright along the branches add seasonal interest on mature trees.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Nikko fir tolerates heat, air pollution, and heavier clay better than most true firs.

directions: Nikko fir is a Japanese species noted among true firs for its unusual tolerance of urban conditions, heat, and heavier soils, making it one of the more adaptable members of the genus for eastern North American gardens. Its needles show bright silvery-white bands beneath and purple-tinged new growth in spring, and mature trees carry attractive violet-purple cones upright on the branch tips. Site it in full sun on well-drained ground and avoid permanently wet or compacted soil, which encourages root rot. It makes a handsome, broadly conical specimen or windbreak tree where many other firs fail from heat stress.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, even rocky or alkaline soil in full sun; Spanish fir is unusual among true firs for its drought and heat tolerance once established.

directions: Spanish fir is a rare relict conifer from a handful of limestone mountain ranges in southern Spain, instantly recognizable by its short, stiff, radially arranged needles that give the branches a bottlebrush appearance. Unlike most true firs, it tolerates heat, dry summers, and alkaline or rocky soils, making it one of the few Abies suited to Mediterranean-climate and warmer continental gardens. Plant in full sun on well-drained ground, since wet or heavy clay soils quickly cause decline. Its stiff, blue-gray-green foliage and formal, pyramidal habit make it a striking specimen in dry gardens and conifer collections.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in cool, consistently moist, well-drained acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; this Pacific Northwest native resents hot, dry, or polluted urban sites.

directions: Pacific silver fir is a shade-tolerant native of the coastal mountains from southern Alaska to northern California and Oregon's Cascades, where it forms dense, dark forests under heavy winter snowpack. Its flattened needles curve upward and show bright silvery-white bands on the underside, and the bark stays smooth and silver-gray even on older trees. It needs cool, humid conditions and consistent moisture, so it is best suited to maritime Pacific Northwest gardens and struggles with heat, drought, or air pollution elsewhere. Used mainly in native plantings and large naturalistic landscapes rather than as a street or urban tree.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; give this slow-growing rarity plenty of room to display its long, curtain-like weeping branchlets.

directions: Brewer's weeping spruce is one of the most ornamentally distinctive conifers in cultivation, native to a small area of the Klamath and Siskiyou Mountains of northern California and southern Oregon, where it grows on rocky, serpentine slopes. Long, slender, curtain-like branchlets hang almost vertically from upswept branches, giving the whole tree a striking draped silhouette unlike any other spruce. It is slow-growing and best sited where its weeping form can be seen in full, such as a lawn specimen or focal point in a conifer collection. Provide cool, moist, well-drained soil and some protection from harsh afternoon sun in hotter climates to keep it looking its best.
sources: The Arnold Arboretum of Harvard University

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; this large Himalayan spruce needs ample space for its long, trailing branchlets to drape freely.

directions: Himalayan spruce, also sold as Morinda spruce, is a large, elegantly drooping conifer native to the western Himalaya, with exceptionally long, slender branchlets that hang like green tassels from wide-spreading horizontal branches. It is among the most graceful of the large spruces and is grown as a specimen tree in parks, estates, and botanical collections where its mature size and weeping effect can be fully appreciated. It tolerates more heat than many spruces but still prefers deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture while establishing. Give it a prominent, open site since lower branches sweep the ground and crowding ruins its characteristic silhouette.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, and handle with care; tigertail spruce needles are unusually sharp and stiff.

directions: Tigertail spruce is a Japanese species named for its stout, outward-curving branches lined with exceptionally rigid, sharply pointed needles that make it one of the most painfully spine-tipped conifers grown in gardens. Its stiff habit and glossy, pale cones give it a coarse but distinctive texture that sets it apart from the softer-needled spruces more commonly planted. Site it away from paths and play areas given how sharp the foliage is, and grow it in full sun on well-drained soil with moderate, consistent moisture. It is slower growing and less common than most garden spruces, valued mainly by conifer collectors for its unusual texture.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring near streambanks or in consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; water birch naturally colonizes riparian corridors across the interior West.

directions: Water birch is a multi-stemmed, often shrubby small tree native to streambanks and wet meadows across the interior western United States and Canada, easily told apart from paper birch by its shiny, dark reddish-brown bark that does not peel into white sheets. It is a key streamside stabilizer in its native range, holding soil along creeks and providing cover and browse for wildlife. Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to light shade, mimicking the riparian zones where it naturally thrives, and expect a shorter-lived, fast-growing tree compared to upland birches. It is increasingly used in native plant and restoration plantings for erosion control along waterways in dry climates.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this Japanese species is grown chiefly for its dark, furrowed, cherry-like bark rather than fall color.

directions: Japanese cherry birch is a handsome Asian relative of the American sweet birch, sharing its wintergreen-scented twigs but developing dark, scaly, furrowed bark that looks more like a mature black cherry than a typical smooth-barked birch. It makes a sturdy, long-lived shade tree with glossy, deep green leaves that turn yellow in fall, and it is less prone to the bronze birch borer problems that plague many white-barked birches in cultivation. Grow it in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, and treat it as a specimen or shade tree valued more for bark texture and toughness than seasonal color. It remains uncommon outside specialty tree nurseries and botanical collections despite its good garden performance.
